title: Al-Majid, the Most Glorious
tomorrow: what does rain on dry ground have to do with the end?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Al-Wadud, the Loving, and the line: loving. Love with hands, waiting past the turn back. Today, two ways of giving glory back.

A stadium chanting one name. A friend whispering wow at a sunset. Same feeling, different volume. Muslims glorify God both ways, out loud together and quietly alone, and scholars have weighed which is better. At the center is today's Name, Al-Majid, the Most Glorious. In Surah Hud, angels visit Ibrahim's house and tell his wife Sarah, old and astonished, that she'll have a son. She laughs. And they answer her: "Lo! He is Owner of Praise, Owner of Glory!"
screen: `A STADIUM, A WHISPER.` → `SARAH LAUGHS.` → `OWNER OF PRAISE, OWNER OF GLORY.`

segments.voice: That pair, Hamid and Majid, comes back at the close of the salawat, the blessing on the Prophet taught in Sahih al-Bukhari: innaka hamidun majid, you are praised and glorious. So how do you give glory back? Here's the first view: under your breath. Surah Al-A'raf says: "remember thy Lord within thyself humbly and with awe, below thy breath." Once on a journey, when the companions shouted Allahu akbar at the top of their voices, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, told them to go easy on themselves: you're not calling someone deaf or absent; the one you call is near, and hears. Scholars on this side say quiet glory keeps the heart honest. Nobody's performing. It's the glory you'd give if no one would ever know. Now the second view: out loud, together. A hadith qudsi in Sahih al-Bukhari says: whoever remembers Me in a gathering, I remember them in a better gathering. And Ibn Abbas reports that raising voices in dhikr after the obligatory prayer was done in the Prophet's time. Scholars on this side say a shared voice carries people who can't carry themselves that day. In a room saying it at once, the tired voices ride on the strong ones. Both views stand on hadith, and both are still practiced. Here's the detail to tell a friend tonight: the Qur'an's own scene of glory isn't a throne room. It's an old woman laughing in a doorway, being told: He is Owner of Glory.
screen: `INNAKA HAMIDUN MAJID.` · `VIEW ONE: BELOW THY BREATH.` · `VIEW TWO: IN A GATHERING.` · `GLORY IN A DOORWAY.` · then, large: `GLORIOUS.`

segments.voice: Say subhanallah, glory be to God, three times: once out loud, once in a whisper, lips barely moving, once only in your mind. Notice which one sounds most like yours today. Then let the sit be the quiet after the last one.
Al-Majid. The Most Glorious: Owner of Praise, Owner of Glory, named to a laughing woman in a doorway. Name forty-eight.
One line to keep: glorious, out loud or under your breath, and it reaches the same place. Day ninety-six.

howItsDone: Muslims glorify Allah in dhikr, alone and quietly or together aloud, and close the salawat in the prayer with innaka hamidun majid; communities and schools differ on how loud dhikr should be.

match.prompt: two views of glory — tap the pairs.
pairs: told: He is Owner of Glory

myth: Islamic sources allow only silent dhikr
hadith support quiet remembrance and also voices raised in dhikr after prayer (Ibn Abbas, Sahih al-Bukhari).
'Owner of Praise, Owner of Glory' is said to Sarah in Surah Hud
11:73, after she laughs at the news of a son.
hamid and majid close the salawat taught in Sahih al-Bukhari
innaka hamidun majid: you are praised and glorious.

fork.setup: you love the loud dhikr circle after Friday prayer. your friend prefers silent dhikr at home. what's the strongest case for her side?
options: 'He is near and hears; quiet glory keeps the heart honest, with no one performing.'
'loud dhikr is forbidden in every school, so hers is the only right way.'
'silence is better because God dislikes noise of any kind.'
fork.reveal: the quiet side rests on 7:205 and the hadith 'you're not calling someone deaf or absent'. the loud side has its own: the better gathering, and Ibn Abbas on voices after prayer. both stand on hadith.

original.note: Arabic: the Most Glorious. 11:73 pairs it with al-Hamid: Owner of Praise, Owner of Glory.

trapdoor: what you thought: glory means bright lights and a throne.
what it means: the One whose glory is told to a laughing old woman, and given back loud or quiet.
what a scholar hears: hamidun majid closes 11:73 and the salawat (Sahih al-Bukhari); the volume of dhikr is weighed using 7:205, the 'not deaf or absent' hadith, and Ibn Abbas on dhikr after prayer.

chat.says: mock interview. kayla says brag about my robotics award. dadi says glory belongs to Allah. who's right??
options: Both, kind of. Say plainly what you did; the glory goes back to its Owner.
Dadi. Mentioning any win at all takes glory that isn't yours.
Kayla. In interviews the glory is yours; save Allah for prayer.
chat.meaning: Al-Majid is Owner of Glory. Saying honestly what you did isn't stealing it; claiming the glory as your own would be.
